Thanks for the information on how to pay to get an audio transcription works.

RCA has created some notable hardware over the years that's been largely forgotten.  One of my favorites is the CED video format.  I remember when those players and discs used to be rent-able in the 1980s.  Back in the early 1990s, when I was combing the thrift shops and other stores for "old" videogames, there was a small pawn shop in my town that bought out the CEDs from some out-of-business video rental store.  The shop was selling the discs for next to nothing.  I was in awe of seeing so many of those movies on that odd format in one place.  I pawed through the dozens of crates of those discs, just absorbing the absurdity of so many movies released on a format that was all but unknown by the time I came across them in 1992 or so.

Adam

17759:
I added three Nitron litigation releases from 1983.  These are from:

SEC Docket; Volume 28 No. 1; June 21; 1983.
SEC Docket; Volume 29 No. 1; Nov 11; 1983.

These three litigation releases are from two SEC Dockets released in 1983 concerning the Securities and Exchange Commission v. Nitron, Inc. The complaint charged that Nitron possibly filed misleading statements concerning the revenues to be derived by Nitron pursuant to a contract to manufacture video game arcades and cassettes for Astrocade, Inc. The action with respect to Nitron was settled on November 17, 1983.

What does that mean?  In these three short legalese pieces, you get some facts about what happened between Nitron, the company that made the Astrocade consoles and cartridges for Astrocade, Inc.  You can view the document here:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/nitron/nitron.html#NitronLitigationReleases1983

I found this information enlightening.  I hope that others enjoy reading about this not-too-well-known slice of Astrocade history too.  On this same page, you can explore some other documents and catalogs concerning Nitron.

Below is all of the information specifically concerning Nitron extracted from the two SEC Dockets.

Enjoy!

Adam

----------------------------------------

SEC Docket, Excerpts.
SEC Docket; Volume 28 No. 1; June 21; 1983.
SEC Docket; Volume 29 No. 1; Nov 11; 1983.
Nitron Litigation Releases, No. 10147 (September 30, 1983), 10202 (November 17, 1983), and 10259 (January 12, 1984)


Litigation Release No. 10147/September 30, 1983

SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE COMMISSION v. NITRON, INC. AND SAMUEL NISSIM United States District Court for the District of Columbia, Civil Action No. 83-2872

The Securities and Exchange Commission announced the filing on September 29 of a civil injunctive action in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia against Nitron, Inc., a manufacturer of semiconductor devices located in Cupertino, California, and Samuel Nissim, a director of Nitron who served as its president and chairman until 1983. The complaint charges that Nitron and Nissim filed or caused to be filed with the Commission and released or caused to be released to the public, materially false and misleading statements concerning the revenues to be derived by Nitron pursuant to a contract to manufacture video game arcades and cassettes for Astrocade, Inc., a privately-held seller of home video games, concerning the substance and purpose of certain agreements between Nitron and Astrocade, and concerning the financial condition of Nitron and Astrocade. Nitron was also charged with failing to file an annual report and several periodic reports with the Commission during 1982 and 1983.

In connection with these charges, the complaint alleges that on March 18, 1982, Nitron announced the signing of a contract with Astrocade which it expected to generate $32 million in revenues by the end of 1982 and $72 million during 1983, without disclosing that both Nitron and Astrocade would require substantial new financing in order to fund the project and that Astrocade's obligation to pay for the products manufactured by Nitron was contingent upon Astrocade's sale of the products. Nitron also failed, according to the Commission's allegations, to correct its projections when substantial problems developed with the contract due, among other things, to Astrocade's financial difficulties. The complaint further alleges that Nitron made less than $7 million in sales to Astrocade prior to December 31,1982, by which time Astrocade had filed a petition to reorganize under Chapter XI of the Bankruptcy Reform Act.

In filing the action, the Commission seeks permanent injunctions against Nitron and Nissim from violations of the antifraud and reporting provisions of the federal securities laws.


------------------------------------------


Litigation Release No. 10202/November 17, 1983

SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE COMMISSION v. NITRON, INC. AND SAMUEL NISSIM United States District Court for the District of Columbia, Civil Action No. 83-2872

The Securities and Exchange Commission announced today the settlement of a civil injunctive action filed on September 29, against Nitron, Inc. a manufacturer of semiconductor devices located in Cupertino, California. (See Litigation Release No. 10147; September 30, 1983). Nitron, without admitting or denying any of the allegations in the complaint, consented to the entry of an order permanently enjoining it from violating certain reporting and anti-fraud provisions of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.

The complaint charged that Nitron and Samuel Nissim, a director of Nitron who served as Nitron's president and chairman until 1983 filed or caused to be filed with the Commission and released or caused to be released to the public, materially false and misleading statements concerning the revenues to be derived by Nitron pursuant to a contract to manufacture video game arcades and cassettes for Astrocade, Inc., a privately-held seller of home video games, concerning the substance and purpose of certain agreements between Nitron and Astrocade, and concerning the financial condition of Nitron and Astrocade. Nitron was also charged with failing to timely file an annual report and several periodic reports with the Commission during 1982 and 1983.

The action is still pending with respect to defendant Nissim, against whom the Commission seeks a permanent injunction from violations of the antifraud and reporting provisions of the federal securities laws.


------------------------------------------


Litigation Release No. 10259/January 12, 1984

SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE COMMISSION v. NITRON, INC. AND SAMUEL NISSIM United States District Court for the District of Columbia, Civil Action No. 83-2872

The Securities and Exchange Commission announced today the settlement of a civil injunctive action filed on September 29 against Samuel Nissim, the former chief executive officer of Nitron, Inc., a manufacturer of semiconductor devices located in Cupertino. California (see Litigation Release No. 10147; September 30, 1983). Nissim. without admitting or denying any of the allegations in the complaint, consented to the entry of an order permanently enjoining him from violating certain reporting and anti-fraud provisions of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.

The complaint charged that Nitron and Samuel Nissim, a director of Nitron who served as Nitron's president and chairman until 1983, filed or caused to be filed with the Commission and released or caused to be released to the public, materially false and misleading statements concerning the revenues to be derived by Nitron pursuant to a contract to manufacture video game arcades and cassettes for Astrocade, Inc., a privately-held seller of home video games, concerning the substance and purpose of certain agreements between Nitron and Astrocade, and concerning the financial condition of Nitron and Astrocade. Nitron was also charged with failing to timely file an annual report and several periodic reports with the Commission during 1982 and 1983.

The action with respect to Nitron was settled on November 17, 1983 with the entry of an order permanently enjoining it from violations of certain anti-fraud and reporting provisions of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (see Litigation Release No. 10202; November 17, 1983).

17762:
Yes, I agree with Ken: Cursor and The BASIC Express were good newsletters.  Between these "two" newsletters, there were 65 programs published in them.  There is a FAQ I wrote that lists all of the programs, here:

https://ballyalley.com/faqs/Cursor_Program_FAQ.txt

I always liked that the programs published in Cursor (both the BASIC and Z80 machine language programs) had full documentation and many also had comments and/or a breakdown on how the printed program functioned.  The Arcadian newsletter often published programs with minimal or no documentation, even when the authors provided it.

In both the Arcadian and in letters sent to the Arcadian, there is some behind-the-scenes gossip about what went on at The BASIC Express that caused it to fold .  Fred's newsletter was out to make a profit, and one way that was done was to accept Bally Arcades for repair.  I guess this didn't work out too well and there were people who sent in their systems with payment who never heard about it again.  This is all hear-say, really.  We'll probably never know the full story.

Why just talk about Fred's newsletter when you can jump in and try out a few programs from it; give a few a whirl!

These are the Bally BASIC 300-baud programs that have been archived:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/cursor/cursor.html

Here are the AstroBASIC 2000-baud programs that have been archived:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/cursor_basic-express/cursor_basic-express.html

Any of these programs can be downloaded and used on real hardware.  You can also try the "AstroBASIC" programs using the Astrocade emulator in MAME.

Just for kicks, why not try out Diamond, by Richard Sonnenblick.  This was published in:

BASIC EXPRESS, THE 3, no. 1 (April 1981): 7.

Diamond is a video art program that is a wonderful example of a very short BASIC program that is visually impressive and fun to use/watch.  It also shows that a person of any age can program in BASIC, as Richard was a junior high school student.

You can download the AstroBASIC program here to try loading on your Astrocade or under emulation:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/cursor_basic-express/Diamond/Diamond%20(AB).zip

If you just want to see what the program looks like when it's running, then you can watch nine minutes of it in-motion, here:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Itw-st5zSoQ
[https://i.ytimg.com/vi/Itw-st5zSoQ/maxresdefault.jpg]<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Itw-st5zSoQ>
Diamond by Richard Sonnenblick Video Art for the Bally Arcade and Astrocade 1981<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Itw-st5zSoQ>

www.youtube.com
About five months ago (in September or October 2020), Rich, the program's author, left a comment about his own program, that said, "That brings back memories. Thank you for posting this!"

If you're interested in seeing what The BASIC Express newsletter looked like, then here is the page on which "Diamond" was printed:

https://ballyalley.com/newsletters/cursor/the_basic_express_vol_3_issue_01.pdf#Page=7

Are there any readers here who were subscribers to Cursor/The BASIC Express?  Did anyone else have any interaction with Fred or the other folks behind the newsletter?

Adam

Subject: RE: WOW Documentation And More
From: Michael Matte
Date: Tue 2/16/2021 7:28 PM

The following is what a portion of my examination of the WOW transfer board has revealed to me. I spent this time examining the board to see if this board was feasible as an optional add-on for a modified hi-res Astrocade. My conclusion is that yes this board is very feasible as an optional add-on. By the way, this board would not be usable in the low-res mode unless it could be modified to optionally add 40 bytes to a pattern screen line instead of the hi-res 80 bytes per line. Maybe all that would be needed is to add a manual mini toggle to switch from the 80 adder to 40. That would be something to look into.

The pattern transfer board provides 6 pattern bit control (manipulation) modes via its output port 7AH, which are listed below.

Direction (shift left or right 1 bit?)
Expand (double/triple size of pattern?)
Constant (0 = use same size, 1 = expand pattern size?)
Flush (set pattern pixels to a fixed color?)
Flip (turn, rotate 45°? Rotate CW, CCW?)
Flop (similar to magic flop?)

Looking at this functions list, it seems that this board really doesn't offer much more than the Astrocade motherboard custom chip magic functions. What the board really offers is processing speed.  The WOW Parts And Operating Manual provides a board theory of operation, but no details on the above 6 control (manipulation) modes. I will very likely be able to determine how each mode functions by examining the board's schematic and by breadboard experimentation.

Here is a link to the Wizard of Wor manual:

https://arcarc.xmission.com/PDF_Arcade_Bally_Midway/Wizard_of_Wor_Parts_and_Operating_Manual_(Jun_1981).pdf

The board operates similar to a ML graphic write subroutine. Five graphic parameters must be output to the boards output ports 78 thru 7EH. The 8 bit pattern height parameter must be the LAST output (port 7EH) to activate the transfer board.

The board tri-states the Z80 off, writes the pattern to RAM, then returns control to the Z80.

The board writes a pattern faster than the Z80 because no Z80 M1 (instruction fetch/RAM row address refresh) cycle is utilized. There are no Z80 M1 cycle delays or Z80 instructions executed when the transfer board is activated. I think the minimum M1 cycle lasts 3 system clock cycles. One system clock cycle is 560ns long. So, the M1 cycle is a substantial delay before any Z80 instruction is even executed.

The board utilizes the Astrocade motherboard system clock and generates its own active low MREQ, RD and WR signal lines writing the pattern via onboard chips (digital electronics) which decode, count up/down, multiplex, tri-state, etc. acting like a ML graphics write subroutine.

It looks like the intent of the board is to write directly to screen RAM, but may be able to write to Magic RAM with possible limitations. The user in the Magic RAM case would also have to output the appropriate magic function to the custom data chip magic register port 0CH.
A system x,y coordinate to non-magic (or magic) address subroutine would also normally be executed by the user prior to outputting the 5 transfer board parameters.

This board has 43 chips on it, but less than a dozen of them are paired off and actually used for pattern byte manipulation/processing.

I plan to break down the schematic into separate parts so it's easier to determine how the board functions to process and write a graphic pattern to screen RAM. This building block approach can be used during the breadboard and testing phase of the project. I will utilize a 555 timer to generate a simple, slow 1 PPS (or higher) visible clock tester along with LEDs, used temporarily to run experimental tests.

I have a PC photo of the board's top, but only a paper print of its bottom. It looks like all the chips are powered by +5V.

Did the WOW transfer board utilize Motorola MC14xxx series chips? Yes, it did.

Surprisingly, Mouser Electronics is well-stocked with CD4xxx, 74HC or 74HCT substitutions. These chips typically cost around $0.60 a chip (less if you purchase 10 packs). For example, Mouser is selling the specialty chip CD4516BE priced at $0.56 (10 at $0.445) having over 1600 in stock. Compare that price with eBay.

I think you now have a general idea of how the WOW pattern transfer board functions.

Bye.
MCM

17792:
I added a 2000-baud version of the "Bally BASIC Sampler" tape that can now be loaded using "AstroBASIC." These programs were written by Dick Ainsworth and released by Bally in 1978.

This tape includes eight BASIC examples on the two-sided tape: Electric Doily, Electronic Music, Gravity Game, Line Graph, Lunar Lander, Monthly Records, Newtonia '500' and Number Match.

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/misc.html#BallyBASICSamplerAB

I'm surprised that I never converted these important Bally BASIC programs into the format that can be loaded using "AstroBASIC."  That's quite an oversight on my part.  Maybe now more people will be able try out these programs, which are probably the most historically significant programs in the Bally BASIC/"AstroBASIC" program library.  Remember when you load and try these programs that these were the first programs, and for quite some time, the ONLY programs, that Bally BASIC users could use unless they wrote BASIC programs themselves.

The following eight programs are on the two-sided tape.

Side 1:

1. Electric Doily (Video Art/Graphics) - Places a random square on the screen and reflects it eight times to create a symmetrical pattern.  A continuous pattern is generated with musical notes.

2. Line Graph - Draws a line graph to match the numbers you input.  Input the number of items you wish to graph.  For each item, input a number between one and 87.  The graph is drawn after the last item is entered.

3. Monthly Records [Not Usable] - A bar graph shows month-to-month levels of amounts which you input.  For each month, input a number between one and 87.  The graph is drawn after the last item is entered.

4. Electronic Music - Uses the musical tones in your Arcade to create electronic music.  Music plays and program returns to menu.  This program sounds different in "AstroBASIC" when compared to when it runs in Bally BASIC.

5. Number Match - Guessing games are a favorite among programmers because they are short and easy to understand.  See your programming course for details.  The computer lists the program and then picks a number from one to ten.  Input your guess.  If MORE or LESS appears, guess again.  After you get the right number, the computer picks another number for you to match.

Side 2:

1. Lunar Lander - Land on the moon with this computer simulation.  When the Lunar Lander appears, use the trigger on hand control one to fire rockets.  The numbers on the screen show fuel left, altitude, and speed.  Try to land at low speed or land in an open area to use as little fuel as possible.  [You can't crash in this game.]

2. Gravity Game - As your skill improves with practice, this game gets more difficult.  Use the trigger on hand control number one to keep the dot on the screen.  If you let the dot fall, your skill level goes down.  If you carry the dot across the screen to the right edge, Skill Level is added to Score and the dots gets heavier.  Score is displayed at the end.

3. Newtonia '500' - Fly a ship where there is no gravity or friction and see how Sir Isaac Newton's laws operate.  Move joystick number one left, right, up and down to fire control rockets.  Pull the trigger if you want to leave a trail.

It was fun to archive these programs.  Enjoy!

17798:
Yeah, Bally Alley has so much primary source material now, it absolutely makes sense that a historian interested in video games of the period would make use of it.

I tend to think that the modern indie game scene was inevitable given the development of computer technology. But there are definitely interesting comparisons to make. The Astrocade was notable at the time for combining easy development and distribution of games (BASIC and the tape interface), with much better affordability than personal computers. As time went on, computers became more affordable. Of course indie development never really went away, but it does feel like there was a shift away from it as making and distributing cutting edge games just took so much resources. There has been a shift back in more recent years as the Internet and services like Steam and console digital stores has made distribution easier again, and tools like Unity and GameMaker have made development easier for individuals or small teams.

Paul
17799:
I can surely say that based on the Magfest talk I did with Rachel Weil last year about the Bally indie development scene that there is definitely interest from folks who are into indie games today in looking at the early era.

One thing I've been looking into more lately has been the Famicom BASIC scene. In Japan, Nintendo and Hudson published three versions of a BASIC cart for the Famicom that used the keyboard attachment and cassette tapes to save and load programs. Not only have other researchers and I uncovered a slew of type-in programs from the computer enthusiast magazines and newsletters that were floating around at the time (at least among the ones scanned online), but there's implications that people were still making games through BASIC for the system into 1996! There's even some Japanese websites that indicate folks learned how to sneak in machine language routines and access the hardware more directly to speed up games and waste less memory. Really seems like the Japanese analog to the Bally Arcade in that regard. Curious how many people leveraged their early experiences with Famicom BASIC into tech careers like some of the Bally BASIC folks did... 17812:
I added the announcement for the "Third and Final Hi-Res Astrocade Prototype" by MCM Design to BallyAlley today.

This is MCM Design's vision for its final low/hi-res static screen RAM (SRAM) Astrocade, a wire wrapped prototype with a 3 board add-under. The three boards are:

Board 1: Static Screen RAM (SRAM) Board
Board 2: User ROM/RAM Board
Board 3: Pattern Transfer Board

The major addition here is a pattern board based on the one found in "Wizard of Wor."  This will allow fast "pattern" (movement, in hardware, similar to many of the on-board ROM routines that are written in software on the regular Bally Arcade/Astrocade.  This will allow MUCH faster movement when manipulating the additional data required for hi-res mode on the Astrocade.

Think of this additional hardware as being somewhat similar to a "blitter."  What's a "blitter?"  Here's the Wikipedia article for that:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blitter

You can read the announcement document for Michael's new Hi-Res project on BallyAlley.com:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/hi-res_packages/hi-res_packages.html#MCMDesignThirdHi-ResAstrocadePrototype

I also announced this in the AtariAge Hi-Res thread:

https://atariage.com/forums/topic/254592-hi-res-bally-arcadeastrocade-correspondence/?do=findComment&comment=4756322

This is a major project-- and one that I don't think I ever expected to see come along for this system.

17814:
Yesterday, I finished reading "The Multiplayer Game," Kevin Impellizeri's dissertation which he finished in 2019.  This 400-page book has five chapters; I read the first four chapters.  Chapter 5 covers the 1993/94 "moral panic" controversy that appeared before Congress and involved Sega and Nintendo.  I've read about history elsewhere and I don't have any interest in it now.

Chapter 4 covers the "Astrocade Underground" and the Bally/Astrocade scene from 1978 to 1986.  It is certainly the best coverage of the Astrocade user groups and newsletters that I've seen written about anywhere, let alone in the exclusive game console world.  There are some minor errors, but these can be overlooked easily enough-- most people probably won't even notice them.  I highly recommend people read chapter 4 of Kevin's dissertation if you have any interest in the Astrocade at all!

As a reminder, here is a link to the document:

https://udspace.udel.edu/bitstream/handle/19716/26115/Impellizeri_udel_0060D_14022.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y

Nice work, Kevin!

Adam

I'm poking around the unreleased Astrocade releases that ended up having copies made and sold by other people (Muncher, Soccer/Shootout, Conan, Checkers, Bowling, Music Maker). 17843:
This is a tough question to answer, Kevin.  I've also wondered who the source was who "leaked" these Astrocade prototype games in the mid-1980s.  Without any proof, I've always figured that it was someone who worked at Action Graphics, but I've never run across anyone who seems to know for sure.  I don't think it was Richard Degler, as he seemed as curious to know who did it as anyone else does now.

One weird point about the Astrocade that, once again, makes it unlike other consoles, is that cartridges were floating around on tape in the early-to-mid 1980s.  These carts could be loaded from tape into the Blue Ram and run as a cartridge from there.  In fact, John Perkins used to send out free tapes with some orders with his work-in-progress version of "Artillery Duel."  This was before the game was released by Bally.  I wonder if they knew about this "freeie" they he would throw into some lucky buyer's order?

It was also possible to load an original cartridge into the Blue Ram Utility, make changes to it, and then save the changes to tape because there was a good machine language monitor built into that 8K utility.  That function of the utility probably wasn't used as often as its ability to load a dumped cartridge.  Still, if one had the desire, it wouldn't be too hard to hack a game on the original Astrocade console.  For example, one could easily use my article called "Hacking "Astro Battle" ("Space Invaders") on the Bally Arcade/Astrocade" to modify "Space Invaders" on a real Astrcade, save it to tape, and then load it back into the console and play it with added lives and the other features that I talked about in my post-turned-to-article here:

https://ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/Hacking_Astro_Battle/Hacking_Astro_Battle.html

One day I should make a video that shows how to use the Blue Ram Utility.  It also allowed you to call up a BBS (with the RARE modem adapter) and use other neat features that one doesn't usually expect can be done with a home videogame console.

Good luck, Kevin, figuring out who distributed those early prototypes.  I hope you're able to figure it out.

Adam

When you see issues with the screen, that's sort of "glitch" video art.  I like it and I've wanted to make a few videos dedicated to it.  Yeah, not many people have an appreciation for it; but for those who dig "glitch video," then the Astrocade offers it up often, and I mean this as a compliment.  In fact, for those that enjoy "glitch video," the Bally Arcade is usually cited as an early example of the possibilities of the art.

When I saw you blowing on the cart edge connectors to "clean" them off I laughed aloud.  You did it to be funny, but it just, I don't know, it never occurred to me to do that on my Astrocade.

As you switched the DIP switches and you said, "On.  Off.  On.  Off," I understood you perfect; I was with you eye-to-eye.  I say the same thing as I go through the lists of games and I'm switching those eight DIP switches as carefully as I can manage it.

"Castle of Horror" was working fine.  When it says, "SWITCH ALL ON," it is referring to the DIP switches on the multicart.  If you turn all the DIP switches to the On position, then that is the "AstroBASIC" cart.  If you had pressed the "=" key afterward, then the game would have started.  You could also have swapped out the multicart and inserted the "AstroBASIC" cartridge.  Either method works to load a BASIC game placed on cartridges (in the Astrocade community, dating back to the 1980s, this is called a "BASICart").

It was nice to see a couple of homebrew games.  I've had the honor to play "War" on the Astrocade with four players at a game festival.  It was pure joy.  The game festival also featured a cocktail version of Atari's "Worlords."  I believe that "War" was at least as good (maybe better?) than the original arcade game.

There is no need to always use the keypad to make game selections.  The Astrocade supports a feature called something like, "Remote Hand Control."  At any menu, press the trigger (you know, the "fire button"), then move the Knob back and forth to select the number.  Then press the trigger again.  You'll never have to press the keys on the keypad again unless you're using BASIC.

Thanks for showing and sharing your Astrocade collection with us, Glen.

Adam

One way to pseuto-calculate the impedence of a driving circuit is the resistance across it. Calculating the circuit that in on the Astec site is the 100 ohm resistor in parallel with the 320 ohm in series with the 82 ohm from either output. The calculation is the recprical of the sum of the recpricals, or Rtotal is 1/rtot = R1xR2 over R1+R2. Thus the impedence of thire output is 82.52ohms. Close to 75 ohms, but still a little off. If the Bally RF cable is 75 ohms, as well as your TV input, it would probably work  OK. But if the RF cable and/or the TV input is 50 ohms, that is enough off to cause the problems we have in the Arcade.

Join me as I open up each box and briefly look through the contents while giving commentary of what is inside these dusty chests of Bally Goodness.

You'll notice that there is some macro-blocking at about the 4-minute mark of the video.  This was added on purpose to hide some personal information.

Among the treats that you will see in this video are:

Bally Arcade/AstrocadeA Look at My Personal Collection, Part 2:Exploring Boxes 1-3March 19, 2021This is a closer inspection of part my Bally Arcade/Astrocade...
www.youtube.com
Overview of Box 1

- Three Audio CDs of music created on the Astrocade by George Moses, among them: "Bach's 15 Two-Part Inventions," "27 Christmas Carols" and some rock music.
- Astrocade S-Video upgrade
- Music Maker/"Music Cassette" cartridge
- "AstroBASIC"
- Treasure Cove (Boxed Reproduction)
- War and Crazy Climber (Homebrews)
- Lil' White Ram 32K RAM Expansion
- Plastic Dust Covers (Bally Professional Arcade and Bally Computer System)
- 3K Art by Stanley Kendall (Test DVD)
- Three audio CDs with AstroBASIC programs
- Heatsinks for the three Bally custom chips
- Working Bally Arcade/Astrocade Console

Overview of Box 2

- Jameco ASCII Keyboard from 1979
- VHS Tape (Samples of Programs Listed in the Arcadian)
- VHS Tape (Hot Rod Bally BASIC Overview by Jay Fenton)
- VHS Tape (Astrocade 5 Minute Tape, 9-82)
- Compilation book with the Source Code for AstroBASIC and Bally Football
- Compilation book with the Source Listing and header file for the Bally Arcade's 8K On-Board ROM
- Compilation book with the Source Listing and header file for the Bally Arcade's 8K on-board ROM (Re-typed assembly Listing)
- About a dozen books that cover building computers and game systems from component parts.

Overview of Box 3

- Astrocade Hand controllers in the original packaging
- 30 original Bally Arcade/Astrocade cartridges in tape storage boxes with third-party end-labels
- Astrocade Multicart by Ward Shrake
- Quadra, BASIC Multicart by Mike White
- Music Multicart from Richard Degler
- Third-Party unpopulated Cartridge PCBs
- EPROMs in a plastic box
- ADS Monitor prototype EPROM
- Two Plastic Dust Covers (Bally Professional Arcade)
- Bally Astrocade 48K RAM Expansion by RetroKidz
- Small box of three common carts for testing purposes
- Boxed, Radio Shack, CTR-121 Desktop ("shoebox" type) Cassette Tape Recorder (Model 14-1128)

In upcoming videos I'll continue to sift through my Astrocade collection.  Stay tuned and please leave some feedback if you find this series fun.

Enjoy!

Adam

17872:
Here is a link to an article released on April 13, 2018 called "Game Art: Copper Giloth's From Video Games to Video Art (1980)"  It features the UV-1 computer in the video (it's sitting under the monitor).  As a reminder, the UV-1 computer uses the Bally's custom chips to produce Hi-Res video.

I just found this article because of this Z-GRASS postcard that has been on BallyAlley for many years now:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/zgrass/zgrass_postcard.pdf

I typed into Google the search term "video art: the electronic medium" and this link came up:

https://www.gamescenes.org/2018/04/game-art-copper-giloths-from-video-games-to-video-art-1980.html

I came across this postcard as I was digging through my collection to make a new video yesterday.

Check out the cool one-of-a-kind joystick interface for the UV-1 computer.

Adam
17873:
The December 1978 issue of Byte magazine has many articles dedicated to the game, "Life."  While none of these articles/programs are specific to the Bally Arcade/Astrocade, versions of "Life," some do directly lift quite a bit of material from that issue of the magazine.  Here's a link to the issue:

https://archive.org/details/byte-magazine-1978-12

Jay Fenton's version of "Life" documentation is here:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/Jay_Fenton/Jay_Fenton.html

Specifically, the entire article "Some Facts of Life" by David Buckingham, is in Jay's manual for his version of "Life:"

https://archive.org/details/byte-magazine-1978-12/page/n55/mode/2up?q=buckingham

I thought that with a re-release of Richard Degler's "Life" cartridge coming up sometime in the (possibly?) few months, that some Astrocade fans might like to get to know "Life" a little bit better than they understand it now.

Adam

This is a closer inspection of part my Bally Arcade/Astrocade collection.  I open and explore two boxes and give commentary on the items that I come across inside.  Most of these materials are from the Bob Fabris Collection.

Here is some of what I unearth in Boxes 9 and 10:

Box 9

0:00 - Overview of the Contents of Boxes 9 and 10

1:17 - A First Look at Boxes 9 and 10

3:23 - A Quick Look at Two New Video Game Books:

- "Missile Commander: A Journey to the Top of an Arcade Classic," by Tony Temple (2020)

- "Who Are You?: Nintendo's Game Boy Advance Platform" by Alex Custodio (2020)

- Three Catalogs:

6:58 - JS&A - Products That Think, Catalog 1
9:22 - JS&A - Products That Think, Catalog 2
12:59 - Chain Store Age, June 1978

16:42 - Spectre Systems Astrocade Screen Graph Paper, 1982

18:59 - Chicago Biographies of an Interactive Life-Style  - Four Chicago artists (Copper Giloth, Phil Morton, Dan Sandin, and Jane Veeder) are featured in this document. The artists use computers, for example the Datamax UV-1 and ZGRASS, to create art that is output to video tapes. (1985)

20:57 - Mark Keller's Handwritten BASIC programs

22:48 - Miscellaneous Documentation:

- Handwritten Note from Clyde Perkins to Jim Fauci about Jim's Blue Ram Unit
- Bally Warranty Card
- "Artillery Duel" Prototype Letter from Perkins Engineering
- "Football" Manual
- End-Label Stickers

26:17 - NCE/Compumart Newspaper with the Complete Bally BASIC Manual Reprinted inside of it

31:30 - Hi-Res Packages, 1-5 by Michael Matte - These five in-depth documents were created in 1986. They explain how to upgrade a Bally Arcade/Astrocade from the "Consumer Mode," which uses the low-resolution display (160x102 pixels), to "Commercial Mode," which uses the high-resolution mode (320x204 pixels) used in arcade games such as Gorf and Wizard of Wor.

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/hi-res_packages/hi-res_packages.html

https://atariage.com/forums/topic/254592-hi-res-bally-arcadeastrocade-correspondence/

Notes from YouTube Video:

This 5 part series by MCMs Astrocades reveals a mystery hidden from the Astrocade community for a long time. Documentation for both of MCM Design's Astrocades, which have been modified to run in low or high graphic resolution, has been archived on the Bally Alley website. The hi-res capability has also been mentioned, in various ways, on the Astrocade community's discussion group website. However, no one other than MCM Design, has actually seen either of these 2 Astrocades operate in hi-res, until now.

The 5 part series is broken down as follows:

1. DRAM Astrocade Runs Low/Hi-Res Programs
2. SRAM Astrocade Runs Low/Hi-Res Programs
3. The Hi-Res Multipage Test Demo
4. Disassembling the Hi-Res DRAM Astrocade
5. Disassembling the Hi-Res SRAM Astrocade

The standard Astrocade will display a screen area of 160 x 102 pixels. That's 160 pixels wide by 102 lines of pixels high, an area of 160 x 102 = 16,320 pixels. A pixel (picture element) is a very difficult to see tiny square (or rectangle) on the screen that can be set to a specific color by the digital device's programmable hardware. This is how text, photos and graphics on the screen are displayed, by manipulating all those pixels with specific colors.

An Astrocade modified to operate in hi-res will display a screen area of 320 x 204 pixels, totaling 65,280 pixels. That's 4 times as many pixels compared to low-res, allowing more detailed graphics to be displayed on a screen.

This part 1 video hopefully, will convince the viewer that MCM Design's original modified for hi-res DRAM Astrocade flawlessly runs in low or high resolution. The viewer will see the more interesting hi-res graphic programs created by MCM Design. Viewing of each program will be brief because MCMs Astrocades will provide longer views along with commentaries later in upcoming videos. This part 1 video is merely a sneak peek at the hi-res graphic programs.

Michael ran into quite a few editing issues that he found extremely frustrating while making this video.  Here is what he told me personally about the making of this video:

----------------------------------------

This video was a very difficult project to complete because of the multiple issues that occurred. My camera was set up to record in standard resolution, 640x480 @ 30fps. I didn't really gain anything visually by recording in full HD. The video parts A, B and C recordings are being edited using Windows Live Movie Maker, which will save the edited recordings as a WMV file in standard resolution with a 4:3 aspect ratio. I'm hoping these videos will generate some interest within the Astrocade community for a low/hi-res Astrocade.

[A person] has emailed me with a conditional desire to design/create professional grade PC boards relating to a modified hi-res Astrocade. I understand that there likely would not be Astrocade users interested in a hi-res multipager or pattern transfer board because of the lack of software support. So, I'm thinking, a single add-under PC board with 16KB screen SRAM, user SRAM and a hi-res ROM (EEPROM, EPROM) would likely be more desirable. I can already think of 5 PC board projects relating to a hi-res Astrocade that are possibilities for interested hi-res Astrocade users. Of course, someone would have to modify the Astrocade motherboard. I guess that would be me who would charge a certain fee to make the required modification.

I'm likely going to start building my final hi-res Astrocade with a 3 board add-under sometime in this coming May. This project will be well documented including videos.

I hope you like this new video. I think it's pretty cool considering it's my first attempt at recording a live TV screen and the fact that I used a poor man's editor.

Bye.
MCM

Notes from YouTube Video:

This 5 part series by MCMs Astrocades reveals a mystery hidden from the Astrocade community for a long time. Documentation for both of MCM Design's Astrocades, which have been modified to run in low or high graphic resolution, has been archived on the Bally Alley website. The hi-res capability has also been mentioned, in various ways, on the Astrocade community's discussion group website. However, no one other than MCM Design, has actually seen either of these 2 Astrocades operate in hi-res, until now.

The 5 part series is broken down as follows:

1. DRAM Astrocade Runs Low/Hi-Res Programs
2. SRAM Astrocade Runs Low/Hi-Res Programs
3. The Hi-Res Multipage Test Demo
4. Disassembling the Hi-Res DRAM Astrocade
5. Disassembling the Hi-Res SRAM Astrocade

The standard Astrocade will display a screen area of 160 x 102 pixels. That's 160 pixels wide by 102 lines of pixels high, an area of 160 x 102 = 16,320 pixels. A pixel (picture element) is a very difficult to see tiny square (or rectangle) on the screen that can be set to a specific color by the digital device's programmable hardware. This is how text, photos and graphics on the screen are displayed, by manipulating all those pixels with specific colors.

An Astrocade modified to operate in hi-res will display a screen area of 320 x 204 pixels, totaling 65,280 pixels. That's 4 times as many pixels compared to low-res, allowing more detailed graphics to be displayed on a screen.

This part 1 video hopefully, will convince the viewer that MCM Design's original modified for hi-res DRAM Astrocade flawlessly runs in low or high resolution. The viewer will see the more interesting hi-res graphic programs created by MCM Design. Viewing of each program will be brief because MCMs Astrocades will provide longer views along with commentaries later in upcoming videos. This part 1 video is merely a sneak peek at the hi-res graphic programs.

(A COMPLETE overview of this video follows this general description.)

This is part of my continuing inspection of my Bally Arcade/Astrocade collection.

0:00 - Bob Fabris Collection, Box 1, Part 6

2:29 - Overview of the folders that were covered in the last episode (Box 1, Part 5)

3:12 - Overview of the five folders covered in this video

5:01 - Folder labeled as "Mail for Tom"

This is mail that was forwarded to, most likely, Tom Woods.

- A letter from Doug Marker from around 1979 from Auckland, New Zealand.  He discusses how he is working on a PAL modulator for his Bally Arcade so that he can get color output from his unit.
 - A photocopy of an article called Integrated TV Video Modulation System," by Wilcox from the February 1977 issue of "IEEE Transaction of Consumer Electronics."
- Bally Home Video Game Expansion Unit Requirements
- Bally "ASCII" handwritten code chart
- Handwritten notes by Bob Fabris
- Letter to Bob Fabris from December 28, 1979 from Charles Nelson.  This is a detailed response to survey questions asked in the Arcadian.

15:29 - Folder labeled as "Bally-Apple Interface"

- Letter to Bob Fabris from Bob Wiseman, dated February 3, 1981, explaining that he has written software that can store and load Bally programs to and from an Apple II disk drive, use the Apple II keyboard on the Bally, and print Bally programs on an Apple printer
- A follow-up letter from Bob Wiseman, dated February 12, 1981
- Apple BASIC file handler for the Bally Arcade.  This is a BASIC listing and it also shows an example of use.
- Bally/Apple Interface documentation
- Bally/Apple Interface source code

22:07 - Folder labeled as "Letters Answered"

- Letter from Dave Stocker, dated April 23, 1979, to Bob Fabris.  Dave talks about his two tapes: Set I and Set II.
- Handwritten letter from Brett Bilbrey, dated April 14 (it is probably from 1979).  Brett mentions the first meeting of what will become the Michigan User Group for the Bally.  Many of the people in the new group met because of programming mistakes found in Brett's Simon game that was published in the Arcadian.
- Guy McLimore's letter to Bob Fabris, dated April 5, 1979, from ABC Hobbycraft.

27:25 - Folder labeled as "Letters Answered.  Awaiting Reply"

- Handwritten notes by Bob Fabris
- "Hot" letter to Bob Fabris from Ted Nevins received in October 1979.  This person's company helped design and manufacture the RF modulator in the Bally Arcade.  He wonders if Bob would like access to confidential Z80 source code located in the 4 ROMs on the Bally's motherboard.

29:51 - Folder labeled as "Arcadian Bulletin"

- List of people who get Arcadians newsletter, the precursor to the Arcadian.
- March 1978 letter that updates readers on the release of Arcadians #5.
- Handwritten BASIC listings for several programs:
- Memory Dump-Hex by Patrick Scott
- Octal Memory Dump by Tracy Crook
- Octal Code Load by Tracy Crook
- Memory Dumper-Binary by Max Manowski
- Memory Contents by John Sweeny
- Postcard with an early Bally Arcade serial number.
- Letter from Max Manowski from 1978.  He talks about using his disassembler program to find undocumented Bally BASIC functions such as ABS, STOP, CALL and others.

35:26 - Folder labeled as "Keyboard Schemes"

- Letter from Tom Johnson, dated April 9, 1979, about how he is working on a full-size keyboard for the Bally Arcade.
- A letter from Pete Wishart that contains partial schematics for the Bally Arcade and the SD Sales Z80 CPU board.  He is working on making an S-100 interface.
- A handwritten draft reply to Pete Wishart from Bob Fabris.

39:27 - A quick look at the top labels of five folders; which are pulled up from Box 1

40:09 - Preview of the five upcoming folders that will be covered in the next video.

Many more videos in this series will come out over the next few months.  Please leave some feedback if you find this series fun or if you have any memories of items in this video.

Have fun!

(A COMPLETE overview of this video follows this general description.)

This is part of my continuing inspection of my Bally Arcade/Astrocade collection.  In this video, I explore and give commentary on the documents that I come across inside of Box 1 of the Bob Fabris Collection.

I cover five folders (about 10% of the total contents of the Box).  Here is a brief overview of what is covered in this video.  There is much more content covered then what is listed here; this is just a "highlight reel."

0:00 - Bob Fabris Collection, Box 1, Part 7 - Overview of Entire Video

1:06 - Outside of Box 1 and a look at upcoming folders for the rest of Box 1

1:44 - Overview of the folders that were covered in the last episode (Box 1, Part 6)

2:55 - Overview of the five folders covered in this episode

3:54 - Folder labeled as "CALLs"

- Letter from Dieter Heinermann in Calgary, Alberta, dated August 5, 1980.  This is an explanation of the typed listing of the results of BASIC CALLs to ROM.
- Table of contents of CALLs to ROM
- "Best of" compilation of CALLs to ROM

11:45 - Folder labeled as "Arcadians Inputs"

- Letter from Ronald Warren, dated 1979, with attached magazine clippings (mostly of Bally Arcade advertisements).
- Magazine article covering the Bally Arcade Biorhythm Cartridge Demonstration on December 9 and 10, 1978 in Richmond, Minnesota at Video Plus.
- "Consumer Electronics" magazine article: "Bally at CES"
- Mattel Intellivision computer add-on
- Letter from Stan Hoard, dated February 2, 1979, concerning how to store data from a BASIC program to tape.
- Example of Arcadian cut-and-paste layout on blue paper
- Patrick Scott's BASIC program listing of a routine to dump the system memory
- Draft letter by Bob Fabris.
- Typed BASIC listing of "Checkers" by John Collins from March 1, 1979
- Handwritten rough draft of Screen Tutorial by John Perkins
- Bob Weber's short program to save registers and the string to tape
- Ernie Sams' tutorial on keyboard and controller information dated October 28, 1979
- Handwritten BASIC listing of "Digital Clock" by J. Cousins.
- Letter from Richard Nitto, dated November 1978, with feedback that he had to him purchase three Bally Arcade systems before he got a fourth unit which finally worked; includes a photocopy of an article by Tom DeFanti, Jay Fenton and Nola Donato called "Basic Z-GRASS - A Sophisticated Graphic Language."
- Letter from Jim Unroe, dated February 1, 1979, about connecting two Bally Arcade systems together; includes a handwritten BASIC listing of "Interactive Program I and II"
- Tom Wood's explanation, from February 1979, on how Bally BASIC works
- "Original Memory Dump" BASIC listing
- CX and CY memory chart
- Letter to James Jones, dated November 6, 1978, written by Charles Vollmer, the national service manager for Bally Consumer Division
- Photocopy of article called "Bally Professional Arcade" by Karl Zinn, from the September 1978 issue of "Creative Computing" magazine
- Trade news "Bally Computer Uses Plain Language" from "Electronics" magazine February 1, 1979
- Photocopy from the November 1979 issue of "Electronics Today," a Canadian magazine, with a cover that says "Bally Arcade: Game or Computer?"  The issue contains an article called "Bally Arcade: More Than Fun."
- Letter from Tom Wood with "GAME OVER" machine language program written in BASIC from January 18, 1979; includes an explanation with Z80 source code.
- Photocopy of Bally flyer called "Bally Computer System Specifications;" includes a comparative analysis of the Bally Arcade to the Apple II, Commodore PET, CompuColor Renaissance, Exidy Sorcerer and RadioShack TRS-80 level II computers.

30:14 - Folder labeled as "Bally DOS"

- Letter to Bob Fabris from Stu Haigh from 1980; includes RDOS source code and three photocopied datasheets.
- "Arcadian RDOS 1.0" Source Code.  This is a CP/M compatible resident Disk Operating System. This code is designed to interface into the Cromemco software system and is provided with an autoload feature. It will support four 5 1/4", or two 5 1/4" and one 9", or two 9" disk drives.
- Datasheets for the "TMS 5501 I/O Controller," and two Western Digital's FD1771 controllers.

35:23 - Unlabeled Folder [Contains letter to Arcadian]

- Tutorial on how to simulate computed GOTO/GOSUB commands in Bally BASIC
- Handwritten notes by Bob Fabris
- Handwritten BASIC listings of "Simon" by Brett Bilbray and Joe Borello and "Reverse" by Brett Bilbrey and Mike Toth
- Letter from Ron Schwank, from March 9, 1979, with typed BASIC listings for "BATNUM" (Battle of Numbers), "Mastermind" and "One Check" (Solitaire Checkers)
- "Convert Decimal to Hexadecimal" by Ernie Sams, a BASIC listing from March 1, 1979.
- The January 1979 issue of "The Printed Circuit," the newsletter of The Computer Hobbyist Group of North Texas
- Letter from Guy McLimore, of ABC Hobbycraft, dated January 29, 1979.
- Chuck Tomka's BASIC program, from January 20, 1979, called "Modified Player Piano."  This is a handwritten BASIC listing "for learning &(16) to &(23) commands."
- Letter from Ron Schweitzer, from February 19, 1979 on how to simulate, in Bally BASIC, the AND, OR and XOR commands.
- Letter from Glenn Pogue, from April 4, 1979, on how to create SIN, COS and TAN functions in Bally BASIC.
- Letter from Frank Loyke, dated May 1, 1979, which include comments about programs that Bob Fabris sent to him to review.
- Stu Haigh letter with comments about using the RND command.

45:31 - Folder labeled as "RF modulator"

- Photocopy of article called "An Integrated TV Video Modulation System," by Milton Wilcox, from January 1977
- VideoBrain TV video modulator schematic for color or B&W.

47:48 - A preview of the contents of the five folders that will be covered in the next video.

0:57 - Overview of Box 1 the five folders that were covered in the last episode

2:35 - Overview of the five folders covered in this episode

3:09 - Look at upcoming folders for the rest of Box 1

4:58 - Folder labeled as "W" [Wiring Contract Work for Blue Ram Expansion]

This folder has letters from people who are willing to be volunteers, work on a contract basis and/or be paid a commission to wire-wrap Blue RAM expansion units.

- A list of about 25 people willing to help wire-wrap Blue RAM units
- A letter from October 3, 1980 from Mark Stradurge
- A letter from Dick De Forest printed on a Model 20 Teletype on August 22, 1980
- A letter from Warren York, dated August 2, 1980
- A letter from Ronald Richter that mentions building kits from Heathkit, including televisions
- A letter, dated June 1, 1980, from Bob Zielke that mentions the PA1 and PA2 Bally manuals.  He mentions that they talk about the Bally Arcade's Commercial (Hi-Res) Mode.

13:59 - Folder labeled as "Arcade Projects"

- A datasheet for the Signetics NE/SD567 "Tone Decoder/Phased Lock Loop" microchip
- A photocopy of an article from Byte magazine, from about 1976, called "Add a $3 Dollar Light Pen to Your Video Display"

16:26 - Folder labeled as "Mail"

- A letter from John Sweeney, dated January 22, 1978, on Tiny BASIC, Version 3, by Le-Chen Wang
- A letter from George Hale, dated February 14, 1979, with his own, labeled drawing for the Bally Arcade's 50-pin expansion connector on the back of the unit.
- A typed letter from Brett Bilbrey, dated October 27, 1978, with cartridge release dates
- An explanation from Tom Woods, dated December 14, 1978, which lists the undocumented Bally BASIC commands and variables.
- A list, provided by Brett Bilbrey, of cartridge prices from Radio Frank, Inc.
- A letter from Ron Schwank, dated February 2, 1979, that includes a listing of prices for Bally equipment from Schwank Enterprises
- A letter with schematics, board layout and wiring diagrams from Richard Belton, dated January 25, 1979 for the Bally Arcade hand controls and 300-Baud Tape Interface.
- The Bally User Group sign-up form from January 29, 1979.  This is the user group that Bob Fabris created in California.
- November 26, 1978 letter from Joe White.  It includes a program called "Bally Trek," written by his son Greg White, that was ported from MINOL Tiny BASIC.
- Letter from Glenn Pogue, dated January 1979, written using a two-color ribbon on a typewriter.  Glenn is a 15-year-old Bally Arcade enthusiast.
- Letter from Glenn Pogue, dated February 22, 1979.  Glenn states videocade release dates.  He also says that there are now two different model numbers for the Bally Arcade.
- An 8-page, handwritten letter, dated December 11, 1978, from Brett Bilbrey.  He mentions several BASIC programs that were sent to Bob.
- Glenn Pogue letter; includes a rough drawing of Gunfight that has been changed by starting it with a POKE command from BASIC.
- A typed letter from Larry Cosgrove, dated January 24, 1979.  He praises the Arcadian newsletter.
- A photocopy of a letter to Charles Vellmer of Bally Consumer Products Division from George Hale.  He also includes an updated revision of his Bally 50-pin connector diagram.
- A photocopy of the cover of "Computer Graphics", a Quarterly Report of SIGGRAPH-ACM, Volume 12, Number 3, August 1978.  This issue covers the SIGGRAPH '78 Proceedings on August 23-25th, 1978 in Atlanta, Georgia.  This issue is edited by Richard L. Phillips.

38:06 - Folder labeled as "Stuff to File"

- An article published in "Video" magazine called "Bally Arcade Game/Computer" from the column "Video Test" #36
- An article called "Texas Instruments Stirs FCC Debate" from "Consumer Electronics," May 1979.  There is a picture of Jack Nieman, the national sales manager for Bally Consumer Products.
- Trade news: "Programmables: Show Business is in Cartridges"
- A letter, possibly from Tom Woods, from 1979 talking about the availability of a laser printer at his work at Xerox.
- A BASIC listings for "Memory Dumper" and "Memory Loader"
- A letter, dated April 10, 1979, from Tomoaki Minaga from Tokorozawa, Japan
- A letter from John Collins that includes BASIC listings for "Checkers" and "Decode Program."
- A letter from Jerry Caraba, from April 5, 1979.  He talks about a subject which he calls the "lost bit phenomena."

46:27 - Folder labeled as "Insiders"

- A letter from Frank Milaro, at Bally, requesting all back issues of the Arcadian newsletter.

47:14 - A preview of the contents of the five folders that will be covered in the next video.

Many more videos in this series will come out over the next few months.  Please leave some feedback if you find this series fun or if you have any memories of items in this video.

Michael Matte sent me this email and he is looking for feedback:

----------------------------------------

Is It Time To Design A New Data Transfer Interface For Astrocade User RAM Add-On Programs?

To: Adam Trionfo
From: MCM Design
April 2021

I was watching your Bob Fabris collection video 10 commentary and then you opened the Bally DOS file. Your comments activated that creative part of me and I began wondering if it was possible to design a low cost and faster data transfer interface for User RAM add-ons to replace the Astrocade audio tape interface.

I was thinking, when I finish bread boarding the second board for my final hi-res Astrocade project with the 3 board add under, that would be a good time to investigate if one could create a faster low cost interface to save/load User RAM Astrocade programs up to around 44KB long.

Out of curiosity, I checked eBay to see what was available in 3.5" floppy drives and disks. To my surprise, I saw an abundance of low-cost drives and disks for sale.

The Basic DOS file might be a good place to start my investigation. The documentation in this particular file is archived on the Bally Alley website. I would need detailed info to begin any kind of experimentation. Some starter questions to address would be:

Do 3.5" floppy drives transfer 8 or 16 bits of data at a time?
How can a 3.5" floppy drive be used for data transfer?
Is there a standard pin out connection for the various models of 3.5" drives available today?
Are there still available, interface driver chips for 3.5" drives along with detailed data sheets?
Is there any 8080 or Z80 source code available somewhere that can be used as a guide to create suitable Astrocade ML data transfer programs using 3.5" floppy drives?

Another question obviously is whether there is a more modern low-cost way to save/load Astrocade User RAM programs? Floppy drive technology is old, but it might be very cheap and well documented, compared to more modern technology. My expertise in digital interfacing is "old school". Sad to say, I have not kept up with the modern interfacing technologies.

Any comments?

Bye.

(A COMPLETE overview of this video follows this general description.)

This is part of my continuing inspection of my Bally Arcade/Astrocade collection.  In this video, I explore and give commentary on the documents that I come across inside of Box 1 of the Bob Fabris Collection.

I cover five folders (about 10% of the total contents of the Box).  Here is a brief overview of what is covered in this video.  There is much more content covered then what is listed here; this is just a "highlight reel."

0:00 - Bob Fabris Collection, Box 1, Part 9 - Overview of Entire Video

1:21 - A look at Box 1 and how much has been covered so far in this box.

2:26 - Overview of Box 1 and the five folders that were covered in the last episode (Box 1, Part 8)

3:53 - Overview of the five folders covered in this video.

4:55 - Folder labeled as "Letters/Programs"

- A letter, dated February 26, 1979, from Boyd E. Pearlson, a lawyer who uses his Bally Arcade to keep track of chargeable hours.
- Handwritten notes by Bob Fabris
- An announcement from 1978 that Arcadians is going to be publishing a newsletter.
- Bally Game Library.  Tape listing with short program descriptions.
- Handwritten letter from Brett Bilbrey with documentation for Reverse, Simon, The Disassembler, Sin(x) Function and Othello; includes typed BASIC listings.
- Letter, dated March 30, 1979, from James Wilkinson.  This is an early mention of the 3159 Bally Arcade ROM.
- A typed letter, dated March 3, 1979, from Brett Bilbrey.  He talks about the "GAME OVER" machine language program and much more.
- A handwritten letter, from Tracy Crook, that includes two programs which use the octal format: "Octal Machine Code Load Routine," and "Octal Memory Data Dump Routine."
- A handwritten letter, dated April 12, 1979, from John Collins.
- A handwritten letter, dated April 9, 1979, from Robert Strand, in which he places an ad in the Arcadian.
- A tutorial by Schwank called "How to Convert BASIC Programs with Arrays to use Them on Bally"
- Handwritten notes to use BASIC commands in unusual ways on the Bally Arcade system.
- "Sonic Satellite" by George Hale.  A BASIC listing and instructions from Applications Programming Enterprise.
- A letter, dated April 14, 1979, from Scott Waldinger which includes programs.
- A letter from Bob Weber
- A BASIC listings of "Memory Contents - Hex" by John Sweeney, "Memory Contents - Binary" by Max Manowski and "Memory Loader" by John Sweeney
- A handwritten BASIC listing, in red ink, of "Checkers" by John Collins
- A handwritten letter, dated April 16, 1979, from Gary Moser.  It includes a short letter with a revised version of "Memory Dump" that he hopes doesn't have any errors now.
- A BASIC listing of "Clock" by J. Cousins
- A BASIC listing of "Convert Hex to Decimal" by Ernie Sams


19:57 - Folder labeled as "Arcadian Indexes/Bally Check"

- Arcadian index, Volume I, printed January 5, 1980.
- Two more indexes of the Arcadian newsletter
- A letter, dated December 15, 1982, from Richard Belton of RGB electronics.  He discusses BalCheck ROM revisions.
- A letter, dated May 15, 1983, from Richard Belton.  He lists the cost that he charges to repair a Bally Arcade console.  He says that he has fixed over 200 Bally Arcade systems using his BalCheck unit and has had only one return, which was for an RF modulator that broke.

23:57 - Unlabeled Folder [Letters, Tutorials and More]

- BASIC CX and CY command screen layout
- A photocopy of page 374 from Montgomery Ward catalog from around 1981.  It is a full-page ad for the white Bally Professional Arcade for $249.95.  There are also screenshots of many of the cartridge games.
- The announcement of the Arcadian newsletter.  This is a printout on silver thermal paper.
- Anderson Research & Design (ARD) letter from Craig Anderson, dated June 28, 1981, commenting on Dieter Heinerman's change to the Computer Ear.  He also says that the Z-GRASS 32 is likely never to be released.
- A letter to Bob from Al Rathmal (sp?), dated February 2, 1981.
- A letter from Brett Holms, dated January 25, 1981.  This piece of correspondence is very long and it is handwritten in a way that is difficult to read.  It's a good example of handwritten script that can sometimes be hard to read, no matter the amount of effort that you put into it.
- A handwritten tutorial, dated July 8, 1981, by Brett Bilbrey called "Fun with Bally Magic."  This tutorial covers the "magic" registers of the Bally Arcade that allow for fast manipulation of data.  In December 1981, Brett re-wrote this tutorial, saying the new version is a, "better tutorial of the MAGIC register. Yes, the old MAGIC tutorial was working ok. It was just a bad example."
- A drawing with "Screen Layout Window" with commands and variables.  This is for use with, I think, Expanded BASIC.
- A handwritten letter, dated October 1, 1981, from Rich Tietjens with many questions, one of which is about the Vortex voice synthesizer that is promised to be in the new version of the Z-GRASS add-under unit.
- A handwritten letter, dated November 15, 1981, from George Shilling.  He has had success connecting a keyboard to his Bally Arcade.  The letter includes the instruction manual for the RCA ASCII serial membrane keyboard, model number VP-606 and VP-616.
- A letter from Robert Rosenhouse, who is working on adding machine language routines to his upcoming game "Space Dock" for his Super Software label.
- A handwritten letter, dated October 20, 1981, from James Wilkinson.  He has questions and includes a SASE for a personal reply.
- A handwritten letter, dated September 6, 1981, from Rory Wohl, including his short BASIC football game called "Hut."

So I recently purchased a MiSTer unit; for the unfamiliar, it's an FPGA-based device used to emulate computer and video game platforms, only instead of doing things in software like MAME or traditional emulators, it's essentially programming the FPGA chip to rebuild itself to match the original hardware design. Different approach, which for some things (like old TTL games) is easier than software emulation to get right, though since it's still in pretty early stages the breadth of platforms and games one can run isn't close to what something like MAME can do. As a nice bonus, you can get a component cable for the thing that can plug right into a CRT television.
Anyway, about a year ago someone wrote up an FPGA "core" for the Bally Arcade - this seems somewhat incidental (I think they were working on FPGA versions of the custom ICs to get the Midway arcade games running and figured that with that hard part done, they could do the BPA as well) and while I've only used it a bit, it seems to work reasonably well. There are a few holes to plug - the author tells me he hasn't implemented detecting controller converters for folks using the original controllers on it and wasn't even aware that there were RAM expansions or cassette-based software for it until I mentioned it earlier today - but he's pretty interested in revisiting it, as he doesn't think any of these sound like they'd be terribly difficult to add as long as schematics are available (admittedly, I haven't come across any for the Blue RAM or Viper-1 on ballyalley). If we can get the BIOS dumped from the surviving unit at the National Videogame Museum, I'd love to run the idea of getting the ZGRASS add-under included in the core as well now that the schematics for it circa June 1982 have been scanned. The author notes I'm the first person he's heard of using the core, so it's not terribly popular, but I think that while FPGA emulation is still rather niche it could end up being a pretty friendly way for people to experience the platform reasonably close to how it should be.
I haven't done a direct side-by-side with my Bally and the MiSTer running the same software on my CRT yet, but based on what I've played the audio and colors seem pretty spot on. Not sure when he may come back around to the platform (since he's working on other "cores" for the FPGA at the moment) but he tells me that he'll let me know when he gets to it as he'd like my help testing and making sure it matches up to the real deal. Other than tape and expanded RAM support, are there any other aspects of the platform that we'd like to see included at that time?

I can field a few of your questions, for sure. The whole project is open source (https://github.com/MiSTer-devel/Main_MiSTer/wiki) I bought my unit pre-built from misteraddons.com. The price of the FPGA itself just went up due to supply chain issues by $35, dunno how long that may last but it has accordingly popped up his pre-built unit prices by the same amount. Normally speaking the i/o is done with a USB hub, through which you can use USB-based keyboards or controllers (xbox controllers, arcade sticks, what have you). There's a few options to use original controllers available recently, notably the SNAC converters or the Bliss i/o (which is an alternative to the normal usb hub) but as of the last time the Astrocade core was touched those didn't exist yet. I think ostensibly if you've got a USB astro-adapter that'll work, but I am not sure how well. 
As for video out, the MiSTer itself can do HDMI, as well as component or RGB (depending on your cable) through a VGA connector if you opt for having analog output as an option. The machine itself doesn't seem able to output composite or s-video, though more recent cores have visual options to add in the kind of fuzziness you'd expect from an old system running on RF or composite (including the 7800 core the same author worked on). One thing that is nice is that if you do have an analog-out setup, it'll work simultaneously with the HDMI output.
At present, the core is set up to map the keypad on the console to a USB keyboard - this is supposed to also be remappable to how you'd want it, but I had some trouble when I tried to do that. For the controller, the knob motion is mapped to an analog stick if your controller has one, not sure if it can be connected to the knob through an astro-adapter or not. The price of the FPGA itself just went up due to supply chain issues by $35, dunno how long that may last but it has accordingly popped up his pre-built unit prices by the same amount. Normally speaking the i/o is done with a USB hub, through which you can use USB-based keyboards or controllers (xbox controllers, arcade sticks, what have you). There's a few options to use original controllers available recently, notably the SNAC converters or the Bliss i/o (which is an alternative to the normal usb hub) but as of the last time the Astrocade core was touched those didn't exist yet. I think ostensibly if you've got a USB astro-adapter that'll work, but I am not sure how well.

As for video out, the MiSTer itself can do HDMI, as well as component or RGB (depending on your cable) through a VGA connector if you opt for having analog output as an option. The machine itself doesn't seem able to output composite or s-video, though more recent cores have visual options to add in the kind of fuzziness you'd expect from an old system running on RF or composite (including the 7800 core the same author worked on). One thing that is nice is that if you do have an analog-out setup, it'll work simultaneously with the HDMI output.

At present, the core is set up to map the keypad on the console to a USB keyboard - this is supposed to also be remappable to how you'd want it, but I had some trouble when I tried to do that. For the controller, the knob motion is mapped to an analog stick if your controller has one, not sure if it can be connected to the knob through an astro-adapter or not. As mentioned it's currently only set up to be able to load cartridges (as the main author who worked on the core didn't realize there was more to the system) but it seems to work pretty well for that functionality. I don't know if the light pen jack or the expansion port are implemented in any way within the FPGA, as nothing within the core as it is uses them. Oh, and one more i/o thing - there is an optional audio-in jack one can get for a MiSTer setup that's currently used to load programs for like, the ZX Spectrum or other computer cores. I brought this up as a possible approach for handling cassette programs (though the author I spoke with seems interested in finding a way to readily convert cassettes to binary files and loading them up within the core itself, as other FPGA computer cores do).

I think any of these items on the wish list that we can dig up schematics for would be hugely helpful for implementing them. I saw on Ballyalley that schematics are up for the 2000-baud interface, the system's main board itself (including the expansion ports), the add-under, and the Lil White RAM. I believe the hackers guide Fenton wrote up has schematics for the 300-baud cassette interface, which would also be helpful (not sure how precise the timing is for the "chips" on the FPGA core but better to have these things available than not). If there are any technical docs for the Blue RAM or Viper-1 showing how those are designed, wired up and what chips they use those would be incredibly helpful as well. Same with the Spectre Systems ICBM Attack controller design! That may be a good candidate for this as well. Basically since the MiSTer is open source basically having any available and relevant materials readily accessible to folks who can and want to do the implementation work would be a boon.

Happy to pass along an invitation to the mailing list whenever I get word that he's ready and willing to work on the Bally some more. The UV-1 might actually be a good selling point for implementing ZGRASS. There's a number of pretty obscure computer platforms already running in some capacity on MiSTer, as it seems to be a pet project of some of the devs to get those working. Hard to get more obscure than that!

So I recently purchased a MiSTer unit; for the unfamiliar, it's an FPGA-based device used to emulate computer and video game platforms, only instead of doing things in software like MAME or traditional emulators, it's essentially programming the FPGA chip to rebuild itself to match the original hardware design. Different approach, which for some things (like old TTL games) is easier than software emulation to get right, though since it's still in pretty early stages the breadth of platforms and games one can run isn't close to what something like MAME can do. As a nice bonus, you can get a component cable for the thing that can plug right into a CRT television.

Anyway, about a year ago someone wrote up an FPGA "core" for the Bally Arcade - this seems somewhat incidental (I think they were working on FPGA versions of the custom ICs to get the Midway arcade games running and figured that with that hard part done, they could do the BPA as well) and while I've only used it a bit, it seems to work reasonably well. There are a few holes to plug - the author tells me he hasn't implemented detecting controller converters for folks using the original controllers on it and wasn't even aware that there were RAM expansions or cassette-based software for it until I mentioned it earlier today - but he's pretty interested in revisiting it, as he doesn't think any of these sound like they'd be terribly difficult to add as long as schematics are available (admittedly, I haven't come across any for the Blue RAM or Viper-1 on ballyalley). If we can get the BIOS dumped from the surviving unit at the National Videogame Museum, I'd love to run the idea of getting the ZGRASS add-under included in the core as well now that the schematics for it circa June 1982 have been scanned. The author notes I'm the first person he's heard of using the core, so it's not terribly popular, but I think that while FPGA emulation is still rather niche it could end up being a pretty friendly way for people to experience the platform reasonably close to how it should be.

I haven't done a direct side-by-side with my Bally and the MiSTer running the same software on my CRT yet, but based on what I've played the audio and colors seem pretty spot on. Not sure when he may come back around to the platform (since he's working on other "cores" for the FPGA at the moment) but he tells me that he'll let me know when he gets to it as he'd like my help testing and making sure it matches up to the real deal. Other than tape and expanded RAM support, are there any other aspects of the platform that we'd like to see included at that time?

Normally speaking the i/o is done with a USB hub, through which you can use USB-based keyboards or controllers (xbox controllers, arcade sticks, what have you). There's a few options to use original controllers available recently, notably the SNAC converters or the Bliss i/o (which is an alternative to the normal usb hub) but as of the last time the Astrocade core was touched those didn't exist yet. I think ostensibly if you've got a USB astro-adapter that'll work, but I am not sure how well.

As for video out, the MiSTer itself can do HDMI, as well as component or RGB (depending on your cable) through a VGA connector if you opt for having analog output as an option. The machine itself doesn't seem able to output composite or s-video, though more recent cores have visual options to add in the kind of fuzziness you'd expect from an old system running on RF or composite (including the 7800 core the same author worked on). One thing that is nice is that if you do have an analog-out setup, it'll work simultaneously with the HDMI output.

At present, the core is set up to map the keypad on the console to a USB keyboard - this is supposed to also be remappable to how you'd want it, but I had some trouble when I tried to do that. For the controller, the knob motion is mapped to an analog stick if your controller has one, not sure if it can be connected to the knob through an astro-adapter or not. As mentioned it's currently only set up to be able to load cartridges (as the main author who worked on the core didn't realize there was more to the system) but it seems to work pretty well for that functionality. So I recently purchased a MiSTer unit; for the unfamiliar, it's an FPGA-based device used to emulate computer and video game platforms, only instead of doing things in software like MAME or traditional emulators, it's essentially programming the FPGA chip to rebuild itself to match the original hardware design. Different approach, which for some things (like old TTL games) is easier than software emulation to get right, though since it's still in pretty early stages the breadth of platforms and games one can run isn't close to what something like MAME can do. As a nice bonus, you can get a component cable for the thing that can plug right into a CRT television.

Anyway, about a year ago someone wrote up an FPGA "core" for the Bally Arcade - this seems somewhat incidental (I think they were working on FPGA versions of the custom ICs to get the Midway arcade games running and figured that with that hard part done, they could do the BPA as well) and while I've only used it a bit, it seems to work reasonably well. There are a few holes to plug - the author tells me he hasn't implemented detecting controller converters for folks using the original controllers on it and wasn't even aware that there were RAM expansions or cassette-based software for it until I mentioned it earlier today - but he's pretty interested in revisiting it, as he doesn't think any of these sound like they'd be terribly difficult to add as long as schematics are available (admittedly, I haven't come across any for the Blue RAM or Viper-1 on ballyalley). If we can get the BIOS dumped from the surviving unit at the National Videogame Museum, I'd love to run the idea of getting the ZGRASS add-under included in the core as well now that the schematics for it circa June 1982 have been scanned. The author notes I'm the first person he's heard of using the core, so it's not terribly popular, but I think that while FPGA emulation is still rather niche it could end up being a pretty friendly way for people to experience the platform reasonably close to how it should be.

I haven't done a direct side-by-side with my Bally and the MiSTer running the same software on my CRT yet, but based on what I've played the audio and colors seem pretty spot on. Not sure when he may come back around to the platform (since he's working on other "cores" for the FPGA at the moment) but he tells me that he'll let me know when he gets to it as he'd like my help testing and making sure it matches up to the real deal. Other than tape and expanded RAM support, are there any other aspects of the platform that we'd like to see included at that time?
