Over the last few days, Michael Matte and I have been discussing the idea of the Z-GRASS ROM getting dumped.  I told him that Kevin Bunch is talking with the National Videogame Museum in Texas that has the prototype Z-Grass that Alternative Engineering was working on in the 1980s for Astrocade, Inc.  I know that Kevin is hoping to have them dump the Z-GRASS language ROM this year and that they have agreed to do it.  The time frame and method, however, seems open-ended to me.

Michael thought that it "would be so cool if that Z-Grass ROM became easily accessible."  He asked, "Wouldn't that excite the Astrocade community for a new upgraded Astrocade?"

I told him, "I'm not sure if the dumping of the ZGRASS ROM would excite the community.  I'm also not sure if this version of the ZGRASS is similar to the UV-1 version (which supports hi-res mode) or is for the Z-GRASS unit from Astrocade, Inc. (which is low res-only).  It's probably only for the low-res mode."

He responded: "Even if the ZGRASS was low-res, the community wouldn't be excited? Would that be because someone would have to design/provide the hardware to run the ZGRASS on the standard low-res Astrocade? Couldn't the community work as a team to get that done or are they content using Astrobasic?"

I told Michael:

"I'd say that the Astrocade community, much like the Atari community, is content playing games.  While the Atari computer and console community does have new hardware and (especially) software releases, the Astrocade community doesn't have that now.  Mostly this is because of the scarcity of the Bally Arcade hardware.  There have been several people over the years who have wandered into the Astrocade discussion group with plans for a game or hardware only to have their opportunity ruined when their hard-won Astrocade system up and quits on them.  If (when?) the Z-GRASS ROM is dumped, I'm not sure how it will be used.  Certainly I'll play around with it myself, as will a handful of the hardcore Astrocade users, but it will have to be done under emulation-- and who knows when MAME will be updated to support the "new" language."

Michael responded:

"Oh yeah, I forgot about the MAME emulation. But then again, there's the issue that someone would have to emulate the ROM/RAM/keyboard hardware to support the ZGRASS language. ZGRASS being more than 8KB of ROM would likely utilize indirect addressing to extend the ROM more than 8KB. Wouldn't someone need a schematic of the ROM scheme to emulate it? Isn't there also the possibility that the preserved ZGRASS language might have some bad data bytes in it? That would suck if someone spent the time to emulate the ZGRASS supporting hardware, only to find the ROM dump had some bad data bytes in its power up routine or other areas. Sounds like a big challenge to work out the details."

I said, "Yes, the challenge would be great... but so would the reward.  Well, for those of us who care about the history of the Bally Arcade."

Michael closed, by saying, "How cool would that be to see even an Astrocade emulation running ZGRASS in low res OR hi-res?"

Kevin, how are you working with the National Videogame Museum to get the Z-GRASS ROM dumped?

Adam

I can field a few of your questions, for sure. The whole project is open source (https://github.com/MiSTer-devel/Main_MiSTer/wiki) I bought my unit pre-built from misteraddons.com. The price of the FPGA itself just went up due to supply chain issues by $35, dunno how long that may last but it has accordingly popped up his pre-built unit prices by the same amount. Normally speaking the i/o is done with a USB hub, through which you can use USB-based keyboards or controllers (xbox controllers, arcade sticks, what have you). There's a few options to use original controllers available recently, notably the SNAC converters or the Bliss i/o (which is an alternative to the normal usb hub) but as of the last time the Astrocade core was touched those didn't exist yet. I think ostensibly if you've got a USB astro-adapter that'll work, but I am not sure how well.

As for video out, the MiSTer itself can do HDMI, as well as component or RGB (depending on your cable) through a VGA connector if you opt for having analog output as an option. The machine itself doesn't seem able to output composite or s-video, though more recent cores have visual options to add in the kind of fuzziness you'd expect from an old system running on RF or composite (including the 7800 core the same author worked on). One thing that is nice is that if you do have an analog-out setup, it'll work simultaneously with the HDMI output.

At present, the core is set up to map the keypad on the console to a USB keyboard - this is supposed to also be remappable to how you'd want it, but I had some trouble when I tried to do that. For the controller, the knob motion is mapped to an analog stick if your controller has one, not sure if it can be connected to the knob through an astro-adapter or not. As mentioned it's currently only set up to be able to load cartridges (as the main author who worked on the core didn't realize there was more to the system) but it seems to work pretty well for that functionality. I don't know if the light pen jack or the expansion port are implemented in any way within the FPGA, as nothing within the core as it is uses them. Oh, and one more i/o thing - there is an optional audio-in jack one can get for a MiSTer setup that's currently used to load programs for like, the ZX Spectrum or other computer cores. I brought this up as a possible approach for handling cassette programs (though the author I spoke with seems interested in finding a way to readily convert cassettes to binary files and loading them up within the core itself, as other FPGA computer cores do).

I think any of these items on the wish list that we can dig up schematics for would be hugely helpful for implementing them. I saw on Ballyalley that schematics are up for the 2000-baud interface, the system's main board itself (including the expansion ports), the add-under, and the Lil White RAM. I believe the hackers guide Fenton wrote up has schematics for the 300-baud cassette interface, which would also be helpful (not sure how precise the timing is for the "chips" on the FPGA core but better to have these things available than not). If there are any technical docs for the Blue RAM or Viper-1 showing how those are designed, wired up and what chips they use those would be incredibly helpful as well. Same with the Spectre Systems ICBM Attack controller design! That may be a good candidate for this as well. Basically since the MiSTer is open source basically having any available and relevant materials readily accessible to folks who can and want to do the implementation work would be a boon.

Happy to pass along an invitation to the mailing list whenever I get word that he's ready and willing to work on the Bally some more. The UV-1 might actually be a good selling point for implementing ZGRASS. There's a number of pretty obscure computer platforms already running in some capacity on MiSTer, as it seems to be a pet project of some of the devs to get those working. Hard to get more obscure than that!

So I recently purchased a MiSTer unit; for the unfamiliar, it's an FPGA-based device used to emulate computer and video game platforms, only instead of doing things in software like MAME or traditional emulators, it's essentially programming the FPGA chip to rebuild itself to match the original hardware design. Different approach, which for some things (like old TTL games) is easier than software emulation to get right, though since it's still in pretty early stages the breadth of platforms and games one can run isn't close to what something like MAME can do. As a nice bonus, you can get a component cable for the thing that can plug right into a CRT television.

Anyway, about a year ago someone wrote up an FPGA "core" for the Bally Arcade - this seems somewhat incidental (I think they were working on FPGA versions of the custom ICs to get the Midway arcade games running and figured that with that hard part done, they could do the BPA as well) and while I've only used it a bit, it seems to work reasonably well. There are a few holes to plug - the author tells me he hasn't implemented detecting controller converters for folks using the original controllers on it and wasn't even aware that there were RAM expansions or cassette-based software for it until I mentioned it earlier today - but he's pretty interested in revisiting it, as he doesn't think any of these sound like they'd be terribly difficult to add as long as schematics are available (admittedly, I haven't come across any for the Blue RAM or Viper-1 on ballyalley). If we can get the BIOS dumped from the surviving unit at the National Videogame Museum, I'd love to run the idea of getting the ZGRASS add-under included in the core as well now that the schematics for it circa June 1982 have been scanned. The author notes I'm the first person he's heard of using the core, so it's not terribly popular, but I think that while FPGA emulation is still rather niche it could end up being a pretty friendly way for people to experience the platform reasonably close to how it should be.

I haven't done a direct side-by-side with my Bally and the MiSTer running the same software on my CRT yet, but based on what I've played the audio and colors seem pretty spot on. Not sure when he may come back around to the platform (since he's working on other "cores" for the FPGA at the moment) but he tells me that he'll let me know when he gets to it as he'd like my help testing and making sure it matches up to the real deal. Other than tape and expanded RAM support, are there any other aspects of the platform that we'd like to see included at that time?

17978:
Regarding my talking with the NVM, it was pretty informal - I corresponded online with John Hardie, who is the co-founder based in Texas who runs the place on-site. He said they'd be happy to dump the BIOS rom on there, and that was like... a year and a half ago. I need to reach back out to him but haven't done so yet,
As to the usefulness of having it - I think that's the wrong question. There's a lot of truly obscure stuff that's been emulated - RCA's unreleased VIP II computer and the unreleased Studio IV game system, a slew of computer systems from the 50s and 60s, etc. that are really only of interest to relatively small numbers of people for actually using but are pretty good to have from a historical perspective. The add-under/UV-1 are sort of the same boat - the era of the UV-1 being a go-to machine for video art and production are long gone, but from a historical perspective there is value in getting it working. The add-under was some legendary vaporware, and while there may not really be much floating around out there to use it on, being able to access it as a "could-have-been" is valuable. And frankly, I think some of the long-time Bally fans who waited for it have earned it!
According to my interview with Tom Meeks, there are only really two major differences between the UV-1 and the add-under: one, that the UV-1 has a faster processor, so it's able to run programs more quickly. And two, the UV-1 could switch between up to 16 screens at a given time because it had more memory available to it (and could have 8-inch floppy drives attached as well). Between both of these the UV-1 ran faster than the add-under but considering neither is emulated it's hard to say exactly how much faster (and frankly, because the designs are so similar it would not take much to get the UV-1 working if the add-under is running). More broadly, ZGRASS itself is mostly lost (and frankly GRASS in general) but is by all rights a pretty flexible language for creating visual effects. I think it deserves better than to be lost in obscurity.
Obviously some developer with MAME or MiSTer would need to decide to take up the task of implementing the hardware and there's no telling when that would happen, but by all rights we should ensure all the materials are out there to make it happen whenever someone does decide they want to try.

The add-under was some legendary vaporware, and while there may not really be much floating around out there to use it on, being able to access it as a "could-have-been" is valuable. And frankly, I think some of the long-time Bally fans who waited for it have earned it!
According to my interview with Tom Meeks, there are only really two major differences between the UV-1 and the add-under: one, that the UV-1 has a faster processor, so it's able to run programs more quickly. And two, the UV-1 could switch between up to 16 screens at a given time because it had more memory available to it (and could have 8-inch floppy drives attached as well). Between both of these the UV-1 ran faster than the add-under but considering neither is emulated it's hard to say exactly how much faster (and frankly, because the designs are so similar it would not take much to get the UV-1 working if the add-under is running). More broadly, ZGRASS itself is mostly lost (and frankly GRASS in general) but is by all rights a pretty flexible language for creating visual effects. I think it deserves better than to be lost in obscurity.
Obviously some developer with MAME or MiSTer would need to decide to take up the task of implementing the hardware and there's no telling when that would happen, but by all rights we should ensure all the materials are out there to make it happen whenever someone does decide they want to try.

I can field a few of your questions, for sure. The whole project is open source (https://github.com/MiSTer-devel/Main_MiSTer/wiki) I bought my unit pre-built from misteraddons.com. The price of the FPGA itself just went up due to supply chain issues by $35, dunno how long that may last but it has accordingly popped up his pre-built unit prices by the same amount. Normally speaking the i/o is done with a USB hub, through which you can use USB-based keyboards or controllers (xbox controllers, arcade sticks, what have you). There's a few options to use original controllers available recently, notably the SNAC converters or the Bliss i/o (which is an alternative to the normal usb hub) but as of the last time the Astrocade core was touched those didn't exist yet. I think ostensibly if you've got a USB astro-adapter that'll work, but I am not sure how well.

As for video out, the MiSTer itself can do HDMI, as well as component or RGB (depending on your cable) through a VGA connector if you opt for having analog output as an option. The machine itself doesn't seem able to output composite or s-video, though more recent cores have visual options to add in the kind of fuzziness you'd expect from an old system running on RF or composite (including the 7800 core the same author worked on). One thing that is nice is that if you do have an analog-out setup, it'll work simultaneously with the HDMI output.

At present, the core is set up to map the keypad on the console to a USB keyboard - this is supposed to also be remappable to how you'd want it, but I had some trouble when I tried to do that. For the controller, the knob motion is mapped to an analog stick if your controller has one, not sure if it can be connected to the knob through an astro-adapter or not. As mentioned it's currently only set up to be able to load cartridges (as the main author who worked on the core didn't realize there was more to the system) but it seems to work pretty well for that functionality. I don't know if the light pen jack or the expansion port are implemented in any way within the FPGA, as nothing within the core as it is uses them. Oh, and one more i/o thing - there is an optional audio-in jack one can get for a MiSTer setup that's currently used to load programs for like, the ZX Spectrum or other computer cores. I brought this up as a possible approach for handling cassette programs (though the author I spoke with seems interested in finding a way to readily convert cassettes to binary files and loading them up within the core itself, as other FPGA computer cores do).

I think any of these items on the wish list that we can dig up schematics for would be hugely helpful for implementing them. I saw on Ballyalley that schematics are up for the 2000-baud interface, the system's main board itself (including the expansion ports), the add-under, and the Lil White RAM. I believe the hackers guide Fenton wrote up has schematics for the 300-baud cassette interface, which would also be helpful (not sure how precise the timing is for the "chips" on the FPGA core but better to have these things available than not). If there are any technical docs for the Blue RAM or Viper-1 showing how those are designed, wired up and what chips they use those would be incredibly helpful as well. Same with the Spectre Systems ICBM Attack controller design! That may be a good candidate for this as well. Basically since the MiSTer is open source basically having any available and relevant materials readily accessible to folks who can and want to do the implementation work would be a boon.

Happy to pass along an invitation to the mailing list whenever I get word that he's ready and willing to work on the Bally some more. There's a number of pretty obscure computer platforms already running in some capacity on MiSTer, as it seems to be a pet project of some of the devs to get those working. Hard to get more obscure than that!

So I recently purchased a MiSTer unit; for the unfamiliar, it's an FPGA-based device used to emulate computer and video game platforms, only instead of doing things in software like MAME or traditional emulators, it's essentially programming the FPGA chip to rebuild itself to match the original hardware design. Different approach, which for some things (like old TTL games) is easier than software emulation to get right, though since it's still in pretty early stages the breadth of platforms and games one can run isn't close to what something like MAME can do. As a nice bonus, you can get a component cable for the thing that can plug right into a CRT television.

Anyway, about a year ago someone wrote up an FPGA "core" for the Bally Arcade - this seems somewhat incidental (I think they were working on FPGA versions of the custom ICs to get the Midway arcade games running and figured that with that hard part done, they could do the BPA as well) and while I've only used it a bit, it seems to work reasonably well. Normally speaking the i/o is done with a USB hub, through which you can use USB-based keyboards or controllers (xbox controllers, arcade sticks, what have you). There's a few options to use original controllers available recently, notably the SNAC converters or the Bliss i/o (which is an alternative to the normal usb hub) but as of the last time the Astrocade core was touched those didn't exist yet. I think ostensibly if you've got a USB astro-adapter that'll work, but I am not sure how well.

As for video out, the MiSTer itself can do HDMI, as well as component or RGB (depending on your cable) through a VGA connector if you opt for having analog output as an option. The machine itself doesn't seem able to output composite or s-video, though more recent cores have visual options to add in the kind of fuzziness you'd expect from an old system running on RF or composite (including the 7800 core the same author worked on). One thing that is nice is that if you do have an analog-out setup, it'll work simultaneously with the HDMI output.

At present, the core is set up to map the keypad on the console to a USB keyboard - this is supposed to also be remappable to how you'd want it, but I had some trouble when I tried to do that. For the controller, the knob motion is mapped to an analog stick if your controller has one, not sure if it can be connected to the knob through an astro-adapter or not. As mentioned it's currently only set up to be able to load cartridges (as the main author who worked on the core didn't realize there was more to the system) but it seems to work pretty well for that functionality. I don't know if the light pen jack or the expansion port are implemented in any way within the FPGA, as nothing within the core as it is uses them. Oh, and one more i/o thing - there is an optional audio-in jack one can get for a MiSTer setup that's currently used to load programs for like, the ZX Spectrum or other computer cores. Regarding my talking with the NVM, it was pretty informal - I corresponded online with John Hardie, who is the co-founder based in Texas who runs the place on-site. He said they'd be happy to dump the BIOS rom on there, and that was like... a year and a half ago. I need to reach back out to him but haven't done so yet,

As to the usefulness of having it - I think that's the wrong question. There's a lot of truly obscure stuff that's been emulated - RCA's unreleased VIP II computer and the unreleased Studio IV game system, a slew of computer systems from the 50s and 60s, etc. that are really only of interest to relatively small numbers of people for actually using but are pretty good to have from a historical perspective. The add-under/UV-1 are sort of the same boat - the era of the UV-1 being a go-to machine for video art and production are long gone, but from a historical perspective there is value in getting it working. The add-under was some legendary vaporware, and while there may not really be much floating around out there to use it on, being able to access it as a "could-have-been" is valuable. And frankly, I think some of the long-time Bally fans who waited for it have earned it!

According to my interview with Tom Meeks, there are only really two major differences between the UV-1 and the add-under: one, that the UV-1 has a faster processor, so it's able to run programs more quickly. And two, the UV-1 could switch between up to 16 screens at a given time because it had more memory available to it (and could have 8-inch floppy drives attached as well). Between both of these the UV-1 ran faster than the add-under but considering neither is emulated it's hard to say exactly how much faster (and frankly, because the designs are so similar it would not take much to get the UV-1 working if the add-under is running). More broadly, ZGRASS itself is mostly lost (and frankly GRASS in general) but is by all rights a pretty flexible language for creating visual effects. I think it deserves better than to be lost in obscurity.

Obviously some developer with MAME or MiSTer would need to decide to take up the task of implementing the hardware and there's no telling when that would happen, but by all rights we should ensure all the materials are out there to make it happen whenever someone does decide they want to try.

17998:
They are correct. Unfortunately there isn't much footage of Western Gun out on the internet; the game doesn't use a computer processor (it's TTL-based) and as such emulation is a giant pain that no one has really gone through the trouble to do yet. And being a game from the mid-70s, there's not much footage of an actual cabinet online either - that video is about the best I've come across. But it is true that Gun Fight is essentially a remake of the concept with a microprocessor and a different art style.
According to the book They Create Worlds, Jeff Frederiksen had been working on developing a pinball machine that used an Intel 4004 earlier in the 1970s before the idea got shelved (due to a lack of interest from manufacturers), but decided to improve on the system he had developed there to make a coin-op video game system that used an MPU - in this case, the 8080 microprocessor. He ended up developing the first bit-mapped display outside of computer research labs, got Dave Nutting to bring in Jamie Fenton and Tom McHugh, which led to the development of Amazing Maze (as a test program that eventually became a commercial release), and Gun Fight (by McHugh and Dave Nutting himself). Bally had recently licensed Western Gun but weren't a fan of the squished, cartoony visuals, so the microprocessor system was a good solution. It also allowed them to replace the fixed playfield from the original game with a stage that changes after each round.
Interestingly, the first five microprocessor-based games Dave Nutting Associates made for Bally-Midway would all end up being early Bally Arcade games - Amazing Maze, Gun Fight, 280 Zzzap, Sea Wolf, and Tornado Baseball!
